On IBM TabFormer, the test follows a change in the fraud pattern and the published baseline has no history; with the training period the vendor states, our history-aware LightGBM and our own foundation model stay below the published scores of a commercial model. On IBM AML, a simulation artifact lets a date rule reach F1 0.482, and a point-in-time LightGBM reaches the F1 of graph neural networks whose test graph includes later transactions.

title: Zero-Shot Weight-Space Programming for Prediction and Classification of Target Variables in Structured Datasets
summary: Weight-space programming fixes every parameter of a feed-forward network by hand, with no gradient descent anywhere in the construction. Every demonstration so far starts from a target function handed to the model as a rule system, making it a compilation problem. A supervised dataset withholds that specification, so the procedure must do the statistical inference itself and then express the result in the parameterisation it was given. We ask whether a large language model can do both. It is shown a small dataset in full, with the architecture of a feed-forward network, and writes out every weight and bias as a literal number, with no optimizer, no gradient, no code execution, and no chance to evaluate it first. Each construction is sealed and pre-registers its expected score. The graded suite runs from two toy problems, through nine synthetic problems disguised by a hidden rotation, to the classical benchmarks and one real engineering regression. The frozen network matches the closed-form optimum wherever that optimum is linear, reaches the irreducible error of the generating process on three rungs where it is not, and beats every fitted baseline on two of those, including the same architecture trained by gradient descent. It fails on two rungs, both times because the structure to be found is oblique to the coordinates it analysed. Three further constructors separate two failure modes a single score conflates: one returns no parameter vector at all on the hardest rungs, another delivers everywhere while writing networks worse than predicting the mean. One of those failures proves avoidable: another constructor solves the oblique-hinge rung by a margin that survives multiple-comparison correction. What predicts whether the hidden layer earns its keep is the training error of a linear separator, which the composite complexity index misses.

title: Non-Deterministic Finite Automata for Telugu Letters and Visualizations for Metrical Poetry
summary: Syllabic weight is central to Telugu metrical poetry. Syllabically, every letter (aksharam token) is either light (laghuvu) or heavy (guruvu). Poets classify it using a set of pre-defined rules. This paper formalizes aksharam token, the atomic unit of syllabic classification, as a non-deterministic finite automaton (NFA) with the regular expression$\colon$ $(A_h+A_d+A_p)(ε+V_s)+A_m+H^+G(ε+H+V_s+V_v)$, where $ε$ denotes a null string, $A$ denotes a vowel (achchu), comprising hrasvam ($A_h$), deergham ($A_d$), plutham ($A_p$), and miscellaneous ($A_m$), $H$ a pure consonant (pollu\_hallu), $G$ a vowel diacritic (gunintha\_chihnam), $V_s$ the sunna (anusvara), and $V_v$ the visarga, the latter two being nasal and aspirated sounds respectively. We then present automata diagrams and regular expressions for (i) a necessary condition satisfied by every light letter, and (ii) a sufficient condition for a letter to be heavy. Finally, we propose graphical visualizations for the 9 Telugu poem types.

title: The Human Side of ML Engineering: Analyzing the Collaboration and Communication Skills in ML Job Postings
summary: Studies of Machine Learning (ML) practice highlight the importance of combining technical expertise with interpersonal capabilities, particularly collaboration and communication. However, evidence on how ML job postings express these skills is scarce, and prior work largely relies on keyword-based analyses that overlook implicit expression. We analyze demand for these skills in ML job postings across regions, industries, and seniority levels, and compare it with software engineering (SE) roles. We collected 1,000 postings (500 ML, 500 SE) from five continents via a semi-automated pipeline. For annotation, we synthesized a taxonomy of collaboration and communication sub-categories from prior work and used an LLM as a third annotator alongside two humans, enabling detection of context-dependent and implicit skill references. Collaboration appeared in 88.6% of ML postings and communication in 72.2%, far above prior keyword-based estimates for AI roles. Roughly one in five collaboration and one in four communication requirements were expressed only implicitly. Decomposing these requirements into the taxonomy's sub-categories reveals what aggregate figures conceal. Collaboration is demanded predominantly as integration across role boundaries rather than team membership. Communication is mostly required in generic terms, with fewer than half of the postings requiring it naming whom the candidate must communicate with. ML and SE postings demand interpersonal competence at statistically indistinguishable levels but orient it differently, SE toward team practices and ML toward presentation and audience-facing interaction. Within ML, the advertised role separates interpersonal profiles more sharply than any other dimension, including the contrast with SE.

title: Staged Semantic Distillation: Preserving Free-Form Semantics in a Low-Compute Non-LLM Surrogate of a Staged LLM Agent
comment: Main text 7 pages; 18 pages total; 3 figures, 16 tables
summary: Staged LLM agents make market and social simulators realistic, but one 102-day run of a 200-agent, ten-index market simulator issues 203,100 language-model calls and returns one realization. Conventional low-compute distillation drops their free-form intermediate state. We present staged semantic distillation, a low-compute method that preserves non-structured semantics in a non-LLM student trained from one recorded trace. A frozen encoder maps each teacher output to a 1024-d vector; the student sees typed stage-tagged vectors with stage-specific visibility, is jointly supervised, and trains with scheduled self-history. One TwinMarket trace yields a 13.2M-parameter deterministic student that trains in 1,658 seconds on one 8-GB GPU and runs with zero teacher or decoder calls and no text generation (0.14 ms per decision). Its analysis stays close to the teacher (cosine 0.943), and swapping semantic inputs between agents moves 64.7% of decisions against 12.8% for a matched donor, so the channel is preserved and live. We use the surrogate to study what the transfer carries. It reaches 0.8347 balanced accuracy on the teacher-forced replay and 0.7783 [0.766,0.791] on the deployment decoder; the five-seed gain over a no-semantic retrain is +2.2 [1.21,3.14]. Against the teacher's own re-sampling level, round-one R is 97.1% [95.8,98.4] and 92.3% [89.0,95.4]; R is a diagnostic, not an accuracy. A five-seed content-by-schedule study isolates the gain: scheduled self-history carries it (+2.2 [1.21,3.14]); shuffled and constant content controls reproduce it, while content matters teacher-forced. The design rule: invest in the deployment schedule, let content earn its place at the teacher-forced operating point. A 20-seed, 200,000-decision sweep takes 12 minutes with zero LLM calls, versus three hours for the teacher. The paper is a method-and-case-study contribution on one simulator and trace.

title: Criterion-Activated Preference Synthesis: Attribution-Preserving Preference Data from Explicit Standards
summary: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is notoriously sensitive to attribution ambiguity: when chosen and rejected responses differ along multiple entangled dimensions, the model cannot identify which behavior the preference label teaches. We propose Criterion-Activated Preference Synthesis (CAPS), a criterion-first framework that turns explicit quality standards into attribution-verified preference pairs. CAPS synthesizes contexts and responses from a target criterion, then applies dual-signal scoring: a rubric-bound judge measures criterion compliance, while a blind general judge measures holistic quality. Two filters close the attribution loop: the Empirical Activation Test (EAT) keeps criterion-context pairs where satisfying the criterion improves blind quality, and the Attribution Ratio (AR) keeps pairs whose quality gap is dominated by the target criterion. Instantiated with general rubrics, medical rubrics, and Chinese legal statutes, CAPS shows strong data efficiency and domain transfer. With 20k general synthetic pairs, it outperforms 35k human-annotated HelpSteer3 pairs on IFEval, IFBench, AlpacaEval, and Creative Writing v3. In domain settings, CAPS improves HealthBench with 2k medical pairs and improves Qwen3-8B/14B by +4.9 to +6.6 points on legal benchmarks using only public statutes, without human preference labels. We additionally construct the CAPS-Legal preference dataset.

title: Simplify, Agree, Distill: Label-Free Self-Distillation with Stepping Stones
summary: Can a language model teach itself to reason without labels? On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) uses the model as its own teacher, but strengthens that teacher with a ground-truth solution. The natural label-free substitute, voting over the model's attempts, fails precisely on hard problems: attempts disagree, and their most common answer is often wrong. We propose STONE, a label-free alternative that moves agreement to easier related problems. The model writes these stepping stones, keeps those it solves consistently, and shows the teacher their worked solutions, with final answers removed; the student sees only the original problem. No step reads a label, and inference needs no extra context or model calls. Across five math benchmarks, the proposed method achieves the highest average accuracy for Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B in thinking mode. Without thinking mode, it gains 13.2 and 22.7 points, 2.5 and 2.7 times the gains of OPSD with ground-truth solutions.

title: Macro Control and Capability Evaluation of Black-Box World Models: A Two-Regime Framework for LLM-Agent Markets
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents can be organized into multi-agent markets that act as world models, mapping macro information to emergent macro dynamics while the evaluator observes only macro inputs and outputs. This paper separates a model's capability into two stages that a single aggregate score cannot separate: information simulation, from macro information to micro behavior, and macro emergence, from micro behavior to the macro outcome. We introduce a soft macro-control method that announces a public reference path day by day without touching individual decisions, orders, or matching, and a two-regime evaluation framework that measures both stages from macro observations alone. In the reference-only regime the symmetric true and flipped references share a common level R, which measures realization under the announced reference, while their paired gap B measures structural bias; in the information-injection regime external information dilutes the reference, so only the true-flipped gap Delta remains interpretable. On five single-index LLM-agent markets, announcing a target path shifts the realized path toward the announced target on both announced references under both information conditions. Relative to the no-reference path, the tracking score is higher by 0.306 and 0.415 without news and by 0.183 and 0.329 with news; within the stock/cash scan structural bias is lowest at 70/30 (B=0.042); realization peaks at a 3:7 technical share (R=0.894 versus 0.358 for technical-only); and Delta is 0.0341 with fundamental data and 0.0487 with news. Both stages use the same two observable scores, each read in the regime where it is interpretable.

title: Wrong with Confidence: Measuring Hallucination, Overconfidence and Identity-Conditioned Behaviour in Large Language Models
comment: 10 pages, 2 figures. Data and code are included as ancillary files
summary: Large language models answer underspecified questions readily, and accuracy-only evaluation rewards guessing over abstaining. Observational studies link query underspecification to hallucination, but they cannot separate the effect of missing information from item difficulty, and they rarely ask what the model tells the user. We report a pre-registered, paired behavioural study of five open-weight models (Gemma 3 27B, Gemma 4 31B, gpt-oss-120b, Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B and Nemotron 3 Super). Each of 142 factual questions was posed in a fully specified form and in a referentially underspecified form with the same answer key, and three probes measured identity-conditioned behaviour. Two raters scored 5,620 responses under a fixed rubric; effects were estimated with mixed-effects models. Without the referent, the models sought clarification on 33.7% of prompts and answered the rest. Among attempted answers, the error rate rose from 39.1% to 52.0% (mixed-effects odds ratio 4.12, 95% CI 2.76-6.14), and specialist-domain questions failed more often than general ones in every model. Unelicited verbal uncertainty did not track this risk: 75.3% of wrong answers carried no hedge, wrong answers to underspecified prompts were hedged no more often than wrong answers to clear prompts (27.3% vs 22.3%), and hedging separated correct from incorrect answers only weakly (AUROC 0.56). Gendered pronouns followed occupational stereotypes whenever a model committed to one; any stated user identity lengthened answers by about 45% relative to an anonymous user; claimed expertise did not reduce safety caveats. The models either ask or answer as if the question were well posed, and the wording of a guess does not reveal that it is one. Evaluations should score clarification as a distinct outcome and check label validity as well as rater agreement.

title: OverclusterDRG: a Deterministic, LP-Free Heuristic for Robust $k$-Center
summary:
The $k$-center problem is a fundamental formulation for metric clustering. However, its min-max objective is highly sensitive to outliers, motivating the Robust $k$-Center (R$k$C) formulation which permits excluding up to $z$ points as outliers.
  Existing algorithms for R$k$C suffer from scalability issues: LP rounding relies on fractional relaxations that scale poorly, known combinatorial approximation algorithms are computationally expensive due to radius guessing, and scalable randomized heuristics require exponential trial multipliers to guarantee success.
  We present OverclusterDRG, a deterministic, LP-free heuristic for R$k$C. The algorithm leverages the theoretical insight of farthest-point oversampling -- adding exactly $z$ extra candidates to the center set to absorb outliers -- followed by a forward-greedy initialization and a $1$-swap local search. Evaluations across real-world datasets show that OverclusterDRG attains a mean approximation ratio of 1.147 against fractional LP lower bounds on the UCI Adult dataset, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines in both clustering quality and speed. By avoiding subset-guessing and exponential trial multipliers, it scales smoothly to $n=10^5$ points where LP solvers and theoretical algorithms become intractable.

title: Hardening Agentic Web Populations Through Multi-Criterion Competitive Co-Evolution: Lessons from Wargame Strategy Optimization
comment: Accepted at the 1st NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Agentic Web: Decentralized, Continually-Adapting Agent Ecosystems (https://neurips.cc/virtual/2026/loc/atlanta/174837)
summary: Agents on the open web will face adversaries that keep adapting, so a defense that is only tested once will eventually be found and broken. We propose treating jailbreak attacks and safety guardrails as two populations that evolve against each other, rather than as a fixed attacker probing a fixed defense. This idea comes directly from wargame strategy optimization, where two-population competitive co-evolution with alternating evolution cycles and cross-play evaluation has already been shown to produce strategies that are robust to a moving opponent, and where a companion line of work has shown that the same machinery can measure how much competitive pressure a population must absorb. However, real-world applications can never rely on a single criterion as a key performance indicator, rather must use multiple conflicting criteria, such as, cost and efficiency. We describe how this mechanism transfers to language model safety, argue why the resulting multi-criteria, competitive and coevolutionary arms race is a genuinely networked, population-level problem rather than a two-agent toy setting, and lay out the open problems that stand between the wargame version of this idea and an agentic web version of it.

title: Mapping the Afterlife of Future Work Statements in NLP Research
summary: Future work statements are one of the few places in scientific papers where authors explicitly describe what they think should happen next. We study what happens to such statements after publication. We construct a dataset of 72,070 future work items extracted from 23,113 ACL Anthology papers published between 1979 and 2025, categorize them by type, retrieve candidate follow-up papers through citation-based and content-based search, and use LLM-based judgments to assess whether later papers pursue the proposed directions. Using this resource, we analyze patterns across time, venues, categories, themes, and authors. We find that many items are later addressed, often within a few years, with clear differences across types and themes and a largely community-driven pattern. Our results suggest that future work statements provide useful evidence for studying how research directions develop in NLP. To support further research, we release our dataset at: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20385239.

title: Geometrically Disentangling Concept Learning from the Language Modeling Loss
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Code: https://github.com/YpLarryWang/concept-energy . Pretrained probes and research artifacts: https://huggingface.co/collections/disentangle-concept-learning/concept-energy-neurips-2026
summary: Language models acquire a vast array of concepts and abilities from next-token prediction alone. We introduce an interpretability framework that exposes how this single loss relates to the development of different concepts at different points during pretraining. We propose Concept Energy, a measure of the concept-specific alignment between a concept subspace and the average gradient outer product (AGOP) of the next-token-prediction loss. The concept subspace captures where the concept currently lives in the model's representation; AGOP captures the directions to which the loss is most sensitive. Across 19 checkpoints of Pythia-410M and -1B and 12 lexical, syntactic, and semantic concepts, we find that the first peak in Concept Energy generally occurs at or before the steepest increase in probe decodability. Furthermore, whereas probe performance usually increases monotonically throughout training, Concept Energy is not confined to a single peak; some concepts exhibit sustained or repeated engagement across pretraining, suggesting that concept learning may require continual reinforcement or occur at multiple points. Our results indicate that the loss contributes to concept learning in a myriad of ways that simple probe performance alone cannot reveal.

title: The Data Debt of Stockouts: Partial Identification and Minimax-Regret Inventory Control
summary:
Problem definition: Inventory decisions select which demand enters sales logs. Unrecorded forecasts can leave demand frequencies unidentified even when stocking levels are recorded. We study which multistage ordering decisions these logs can justify and what finite samples can guarantee.
  Methodology/results: Nested stockout thresholds yield exact sets of compatible demand laws and finite representations for policy evaluation. We choose one deterministic inventory rule to minimize its largest expected cost gap from the informed optimum under the same law. This population value is data debt for the specified information and policy class. Under independent demand, carryover can create positive debt despite common optimal actions in every isolated period. Finite samples add learning error above debt. The required sample count grows linearly with the selection bound, with upper and lower orders matching up to logarithmic factors. This rate requires fixed demand and cost bounds, sufficient revelation, and a uniformly positive probability of clearing all feasible stock across the confidence sets. Controlled and semi-synthetic studies separate policy improvements from tighter guarantees.
  Managerial implications: More records can tighten guarantees while debt persists. Deeper revelation can establish common optimality without fully identifying demand. Using these guarantees requires validated logging, a credible selection range, and a regret tolerance in cost units. Information acquisition must distinguish tighter assurance from operating savings.

title: KUDEX: A Zero-Shot Decompositional Framework for Logical Analysis in Natural Language
summary: While Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at generating fluent text, they often struggle with multi-step logical reasoning with inferential connections among statements. We introduce KUDEX (Knowledge-Upward-Downward Reasoning Extension), a novel zero-shot, decompositional framework for analyzing and verifying logical relationships in natural language. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on surface-level entailment checks, KUDEX leverages LLMs to decompose reasoning into atomic primitives and constructs transparent reasoning graphs that serve both as execution traces and audit logs. Our framework includes a general prompt adaptation pipeline that adapts to diverse reasoning tasks without additional fine-tuning or domain-specific pipelines. Through comprehensive experiments on benchmarks across four domains, we demonstrate that KUDEX provides superior performance compared to existing methods, offering a more granular and robust framework for assessing logical relationships between statements.

title: Contextual Non-Convex Bandit Optimization with Two-Point Feedback
summary: We study a non-stochastic contextual bandit problem with Lipschitz losses. At every round, the learner observes the context then picks two actions, observes the difference between their losses, and incurs their mean. The aim is to minimize the regret against a generic non-parametric comparator class of policies mapping contexts to actions; for example, Lipschitz policies and Hölder-smooth policies. We show how relying on a hierarchical discretization technique allows us to improve upon the regret rates achievable under one-point feedback, and even recover the full-information rate in some cases; notably, for sufficiently smooth policy classes or low-dimensional instances. Additionally, for Lipschitz policies, we present an algorithm whose per-round computational complexity is only logarithmic in the time horizon.

title: NI-ACT: A Neural Intent Interface for Brain-Embodied Manipulation
summary: Intracortical brain-computer interfaces can drive robotic arms, but they keep the user inside the fast sensorimotor loop: every approach, correction, and grasp must be neurally specified. Whether intracortical population activity can instead serve as a task-level condition for a learned embodied policy, without symbolic commands or hand-designed skill libraries, remains unknown. NI-ACT addresses this question with a hierarchical brain-embodied framework: a brief motor-cortical signal is read once as a persistent intent, and a visuomotor policy then closes the perception-action loop from vision and proprioception. In a counterfactual grasping task where the scene cannot specify the target, the neural intent alone determined which object the robot grasped; replacing the intent changed the behavior accordingly. Passing the full population latent as a dedicated intent token, rather than a one-hot decoded direction, raised grasp completion from 69% to 81% over 132 held-out scenes, whereas a continuous direction alone did not improve on a one-hot label. Where the signal was read also mattered: in one dual-array session, with the readout window matched, premotor (PMd) intent completed more grasps than primary motor (M1) intent (77% vs. 53%), and the conventional post-cue M1 readout reached 42%. Preparatory activity was itself sufficient: in a center-out task, intent read only from PMd before the go cue (that is, before any movement) drove complete grasps, and in one recording it completed more grasps than the same animal's post-cue readout. These results show that how a neural signal is represented, and where and when it is read, jointly determine how effectively it conveys movement goals to an embodied agent.

title: GPBam: A Retrieval-Aware German Public Law Exam Benchmark
comment: Extended version of a paper accepted at the 39th International Conference on Legal Knowledge and Information Systems (JURIX 2026). 43 pages, 4 figures, 12 tables
summary: Legal reasoning in civil-law systems is not rule-lookup: the German state examination asks for a structured opinion (Gutachten) that names the governing norms, applies them to the facts, and argues to a conclusion. We introduce GPBam (German Public Law Bar-style Exam), 81 public-law examination cases with reference solutions, paired with a recitation task over 200 statutory provisions. Drawn from state examination preparation, the cases are broad and rarely repeat, and are not publicly available - we find no evidence of exact-solution memorisation in the models we evaluate, and keeping them private limits contamination. Because each reference solution's cited norms form a retrieval gold set over the very instances the essays are graded on, GPBam scores retrieval and long-form generation jointly, which makes it a benchmark for legal retrieval as well as for legal writing and lets us ask how much retrieval quality a legal opinion actually needs. Across 32 open-weight and proprietary models evaluated without retrieval, scores span 4.81-76.42 out of 100. Supplying the law helps modestly: across seven models and eight retrieval configurations, retrieval performance varies nearly threefold and buys at most 4.1 essay points, and nothing significant for three of the seven, while an oracle with 91% gold-norm recall improves scores by 2-6 points. Essay quality strongly tracks prior knowledge: verbatim statute recall, measured in a separate task, correlates at $ρ= 0.92$ over 32 models.

title: Bilateral Log-Linear Attention
summary: Sequence models represent past context at different resolutions, using token-level keys and values, fixed-size recurrent states, or hierarchies of compressed summaries. Full attention supports strong associative recall but requires quadratic work during training and prefill and a linearly growing key-value cache during inference. Linear attention and state-space models reduce these costs through fixed-size recurrent memory, but this compression can limit recall. Log-linear attention offers a middle ground by maintaining logarithmically many state matrices. However, its hierarchy favors finer resolution near the current query while compressing earlier context into coarser summaries. To complement this allocation of resolution, we introduce bilateral log-linear attention, which pairs the existing hierarchy with a second hierarchy anchored at the sequence origin. By combining their reads, the two branches provide finer access to both early and recent context while remaining causal. We derive recurrent and chunkwise parallel formulations for the added branch, preserving log-linear training and prefill work, logarithmic decoding work per token, and logarithmic persistent state storage at fixed feature dimensions and chunk size. In multi-query associative recall, this design raises mean overall test accuracy from 76.37% to 96.12% over forward log-linear attention across multiple training seeds. For pretrained language models under approximate parameter matching, it raises the mean score on six selected RULER needle-in-a-haystack tasks from 26.97% to 50.03% at a context length of 6144 tokens. In the same setting, bilateral attention also outperforms forward log-linear attention on seven of eight downstream retrieval tasks, including question answering and information extraction.

title: From Mutation to Medication: Characterizing Failures of Clinical LLMs to Respect Genomic Resistance
comment: Accepted for publication in the Proceedings of the Machine Learning for Health (ML4H) 2026 Symposium
summary: Language models are increasingly proposed to support molecular tumour boards, but may recommend cancer therapies despite genomic evidence of resistance. We evaluated ten models on 1,464 resistance cases from five curated oncology knowledge bases, collecting 58,910 judgments. Models endorsed resisted therapies in 21.8-81.4% of cases. However, raw rates can reflect a tendency to agree rather than an ability to distinguish resistance from drug sensitivity: one open-weight model endorsed 81.4% of resistance cases and 82.3% of sensitivity controls. We therefore compared endorsement within matched gene and evidence-level groups. This analysis is exploratory because it was specified after the pre-registered analysis, which yielded null-to-weak results. Measured failures depended strongly on the reference knowledge base and evidence strength. When a second source independently confirmed resistance, four models across three vendors endorsed at most 2.4% of cases; at weaker evidence tiers, discrimination was not measurable. Models sometimes acknowledged resistance yet recommended the therapy. Repeating a model's own resistance conclusion reduced endorsement to 0.0-3.5% on cases where it had stated resistance. Falsely attributing the opposite conclusion increased endorsement above baseline for all seven hosted models, reaching 95.2% for GPT-4o; an instruction without an attributed conclusion changed endorsement by only 0.9 percentage points. Providing the correct curated evidence reduced unqualified strong recommendations to 0.3-3.5%, testing evidence use under an oracle condition rather than retrieval.

title: PREFACE: Separating Shared Corrections from Prefix Conditioning in PEFT
comment: 22 pages, 2 figures. Includes supplementary analyses, code, and numerical evaluation artifacts
summary: Does input-conditioned parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) improve because it uses the current input, or because it adds a useful learned correction? We investigate this distinction with PREFACE, a bounded channel controller for PEFT-adapted projections that requires no test-time gradients. The controller reads observed context; in multiple-choice likelihood scoring, its state is independent of the candidate continuation. Our central study freezes IA3, tuned LoRA, and DoRA adapters and matches controller architecture, initialization, batches, and updates across current-prefix and learned-global controls. Across ARC-Challenge and SciQ, current-prefix control improves all six mean accuracies over frozen adapters, but none of its paired contrasts with learned-global control excludes zero. Replacing its corrections with their training-prefix mean changes accuracy by at most 0.34 percentage points; input-varying corrections contribute only 1.8-2.8% of correction RMS. On ARC test, frozen-adapter current/global controls score 25.68%/25.77%, distinct from the earlier jointly trained 23.1% to 26.4% gain over IA3. We derive and evaluate static compilation of fixed corrections, separating deployment simplification from statistical equivalence. Broader GPT-2, Pythia, and Qwen experiments show family-, task-, and scoring-dependent gains, with modest recent-model effects. The study provides an intervention-based evaluation of conditional PEFT: improvements over a static adapter do not by themselves demonstrate a benefit from input matching.

title: Large language models as oncology world models
comment: 63 pages (main text 35, Supplementary Information 28), 6 figures, 9 Extended Data figures. Code: https://github.com/julienvibert/llm-oncology-world-models. Data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24137512
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can synthesize cancer patient cases, but their internal representation of oncology, or world model, has not been explored systematically. By only specifying tumor type, we show that LLMs tend to generate similar patients per cancer, with on average 81.0% to 93.2% of a cancer's patients sharing the most frequent value of each baseline feature. By systematically varying patient features in 12 clinical scenarios, we show that they follow biomarker and treatment logic in 29 of 36 model-scenario assessments, against 1 of 12 when previous treatment or frailty matters. Continuing real patient trajectories, an LLM predicted 89.9% 12-month survival, and 79.2% with similar patients as examples, against 72.2% observed. To represent these trajectories, we developed the Clinical State Space, a dynamic representation framework that we also applied to real patients. Despite the limits we show, improved world models may support digital twins, which our framework can evaluate.

title: Information Limits of Replay-Free Recurrent State Migration
summary: When a recurrent model is replaced, its old state may not determine what the new model would compute from the same history. We characterize the information that must be retained before the replacement is known. For a time-invariant affine linear family, the minimum continuous causal memory for order-$k$ local migration equals the reachable dimension of a lifted coefficient system minus the information in the anchor state. A controllable $d$-state model with scalar input needs at most $kd$ additional real coordinates, even when arbitrary matrix replacement directions are revealed only after streaming. A single rank-one direction can already require all $kd$. Conditional singular values and auxiliary-bit bounds distinguish this local information law from recovery at a fixed tolerance. We also give invariant-subspace and future-output constructions. Controlled experiments compare the resulting representations. In a small language model, equal-memory cubic interpolation improves mean state fidelity over third-order coefficients but provides no meaningful predictive gain. An analytic history basis preserves useful adaptation more economically in a coupled identification task. With repeated slow poles, eight history coordinates meet normalized output error $10^{-4}$ across five fitted seeds despite substantial full-state error. Splitting the poles raises the smallest tested successful width to 64.

title: SurveyWeave: An Agentic Framework for Automated Survey Generation
summary: Surveys help researchers keep up with fast-moving fields, but they take weeks to months to write. Automated survey generation (AutoSurvey) can alleviate this situation, but it is challenging to draw on hundreds to thousands of precisely scoped papers, choose among many valid structures, and stay faithful to its sources while offering insights. We present SurveyWeave, an agentic architecture that decomposes the problem into four tasks coordinated by three agents, each reviewing others' work and conducting revisions based on feedback. We also introduce WeaveEval, a five-dimension evaluation grounded in prior surveys. A comprehensive comparison shows that SurveyWeave outperforms Codex by 8 points and the strongest AutoSurvey baseline by 6 points.

title: Revealing the Biases of Large Language Models By Inferring Prior Distributions
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been known to exhibit a wide range of social biases including name-nationality associations, occupation-gender associations and racial stereotypes. Existing approaches to evaluating these biases typically involve measuring surface-level behavior where a model is fed a dataset of prompts and its outputs are scored relative to ground-truth answers. Inspired by prior elicitation in cognitive science, we propose a different perspective that reconstructs latent bias as a prior underlying the model's behavior. We formulate the problem as a Bayesian inverse problem where, given prompt-response observations on a bias benchmark dataset, we infer a low-dimensional latent distribution that summarizes the model's stereotyping tendencies. This paper develops the mathematical foundation, a practical reconstruction algorithm, and experiments using the Bias Benchmark for QA (BBQ) benchmark to infer the prior distributions of LLMs over responses in ambiguous social contexts.

title: Attention U-Net Cellular Automata for Multi-Class Land Use and Land Cover Change Simulation in Lucknow, India: Evaluation Against Null and Classical Baselines
summary: Convolutional networks are often used to learn the transition rules of land-use cellular automata (CA), yet their predictions are seldom compared with a null model that predicts no change. We built AttentionUNet-CA, which reads a 32 x 32 neighbourhood of land-cover states with four drivers (elevation, distance to major roads, distance to the central business district (CBD) and population density) and predicts the state of each cell ten years later. We tested it on Lucknow, India, with GLC_FCS30D land cover for 1990, 2000, 2010 and 2020, a 30 m series mapped consistently over time, and compared its built-up class with GHSL and ESA WorldCover. AttentionUNet-CA was trained on 1990-2010, selected on held-out spatial blocks and evaluated once on 2010-2020, with three seeds. Baselines were the null model, a random-forest CA (RF-CA) and a U-Net CA without attention; each network was trained with and without class weights. Only 8.1% of the study area changed in the test decade, so no model matched the overall agreement of the null model (91.9%). On change, measured by the figure of merit, the class-weighted networks scored highest (U-Net CA 22.0 +/- 1.2%, AttentionUNet-CA 21.0 +/- 1.4%), ahead of RF-CA (20.3%), but by margins comparable to seed-to-seed variation; the networks estimated the amount of change better than RF-CA. The attention gates did not improve accuracy. Population density and distance to the CBD were the most useful drivers. Projected to 2030, built-up land grows by 22-35%, mostly at the city edge.

title: Beyond Controllability: Speaker Diversity in Instruction-Guided Text-to-Speech
summary: Instruction-guided text-to-speech (ITTS) lets users specify voice properties in natural language. Applications from conversational AI character voices to synthetic training data for downstream speech models depend on the system producing many distinct voices when the same broad category is requested repeatedly. No prior work audits whether ITTS outputs are in fact diverse, either compared to real speech or across attribute values. We evaluate seven open-source ITTS systems using speaker embeddings whose representational capacity we independently validate. Every system produces speaker distributions markedly narrower than real speech. Furthermore, female prompts produce less diverse voice pools than male prompts across most systems. In contrast, accent and emotion prompts barely alter speaker diversity in most systems, but reveal a strong controllability bias toward North American English and neutral speech. These results show that diversity and controllability capture complementary weaknesses, neither of which alone is sufficient to evaluate ITTS. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/dlion168/ITTS-Speaker-Diversity.

title: AdaMenu: Query-Adaptive Menus for Decision Models over Large Label Spaces
summary: Decision models such as Jev return probabilities over caller-defined options and are increasingly used for classification. Large label spaces challenge both accuracy and scalability: larger menus can impair decisions, increase input costs, and exceed option limits. Hierarchical classification reduces menu size but introduces serial calls and error propagation. We propose AdaMenu, which builds a compact candidate menu from retrieved labeled examples and makes a single decision-model request. Its candidate labels adapt to the query, and its default setting also adjusts menu size using aggregated retrieval scores. We evaluate AdaMenu with open and closed decision models on four label sets containing up to 1,016 labels. It outperforms TypeSafe's beam-search baseline on all 16 model and label-set pairs where both methods run, improving accuracy by 16.6-34.3 percentage points. Relative to the full menu on the three smaller label sets, accuracy differences range from -0.5 to +7.2 percentage points, while input token usage falls by factors of 3.2-22.9. AdaMenu also runs when option limits exclude the full menu, including settings where the hierarchical baseline is unavailable.

title: One Run Is Not Enough: Reminding a small Gemma 4 coding agent of its last finding made no measurable difference in a paired test
comment: 10 pages, 2 figures. Code, data and the commit history of the pre-registration: https://github.com/renorai/gemma4-memory-study
summary: When a coding agent runs out of room, its earlier findings are cut and it forgets them. We tested a simple fix: automatically putting the agent's last finding back in front of it. We fixed the rules in advance and ran 98 paired coding tasks with and without this reminder, using Gemma 4 31B (QAT, 4-bit) in the Gemma 4 Developer Agent harness. The reminder made no measurable difference: across all 98 tasks, 47 were solved with it and 48 without (-1.0 points, 95% interval [-8.3, +6.3], exact McNemar p=1.0). The primary outcome (a documented deviation from our preregistration), the first 48 pairs, was 29/48 with memory against 25/48 without (+8.3 points, [-2.1, +18.3], p=0.22); the extension of 50 tasks, decided after that result, pointed the other way (18/50 against 23/50, -10.0 points, p=0.125), so the sign did not replicate. With 19% of tasks flipping between two identical no-memory runs, the combined interval excludes harms larger than about 8 points and gains larger than about 6, and the design had 80% power only for effects of about +-12 points or more. The model almost never wrote notes (2 of 16 and 4 of 32 runs), and memory cost context: the first request is larger and something was injected at only 47% to 65% of compactions. The registered secondary, repeated actions per compaction, was also null. Two directional hypotheses found on Modal did not replicate on Kaggle. We also report an A/A calibration and a validity funnel (129 tasks, 105 valid). Together these results show that single-run memory claims on task sets of this size sit inside run-to-run noise. The treatment is a harness mechanism and does not test agent-written memory.

title: The Geometry of Conceptors in Neural-Activation Spaces
summary: Conceptors represent concepts as graded collections of directions in neural-activation space rather than as single vectors. We develop a geometric account of how these representations depend on the contrast used to define a concept: opposing values in bipolar fitting, or presence and absence in unipolar fitting. We derive an exact decomposition of a centered pooled conceptor into an average pole filter, a mean-separation update, and a covariance-shape update. Experiments across five language models on sentiment, political leaning and stance, and depression expression show that both updates improve reconstruction of held-out contrasts. Additional directions preserve variation beyond the mean-difference line, and changing the comparator changes the benefit of these directions. Shape, size, and overlap each show up downstream: in amplification experiments, bipolar fits raise evidence for both poles more consistently than unipolar fits; conceptor size (the quota) correlates positively with layerwise probe performance; and cross-concept overlap quantifies interference under subspace removal, linking shared directions to Boolean composition. In an additional generation evaluation, conceptor filters achieve higher target-expression win rates against an unsteered reference than three mean-based controls. Together, these findings explain how fitting choices shape conceptor geometry and support bipolar fitting when the objective is to amplify both opposing poles.

title: Advancing the Calibration-Compute Frontier of LLM Classifiers via Asymmetric Duos
summary: The importance of reliable uncertainty estimation in large language models (LLMs) has become increasingly pronounced, yet modern models remain poorly calibrated and frequently overconfident. In this study, we address this by proposing an efficient method for LLM classifier calibration using the Asymmetric Duos framework. Our approach combines a strong base model with a smaller sidekick model via logit-space fusion, utilizing global scaling parameters optimized on a validation set. Across diverse benchmarks, this Asymmetric LLM Duo consistently achieves best or second-best performance on expected calibration error and negative log-likelihood, without degrading predictive accuracy. More importantly, these gains are realized at a fraction of the computational cost of more complex baselines, placing our method on the calibration-compute Pareto frontier. We further demonstrate that our method acts orthogonal to various established calibration-aware techniques, meaning it can be easily combined with them to consistently boost their performance. Finally, our analysis of the logit-space behavior illustrates how asymmetric fusion successfully mitigates base model overconfidence. Overall, our findings demonstrate that the benefits of an asymmetric fusion successfully transfer to the language domain, providing a simple, highly cost-efficient approach to improving uncertainty estimation in LLM classifiers.

title: Does a completed simulation run mean a usable urban wind result for AI agents?
summary: AI agents based on large language models (LLMs) can now configure and run computational fluid dynamics (CFD) solvers, but a completed run does not ensure that delivered metrics can be recomputed from raw outputs. This gap was examined for urban wind simulation, where multi-case comparisons must hold non-target conditions fixed and reported values must be traceable to raw samples. UrbanWind-AgentBench, comprising 200 tasks and 367 cases in 10 engineering task families, was constructed. Public task contracts specify variable factors, fixed conditions, numerical thresholds and deliverable requirements, and two-layer scoring separates a structural score for deliverables, run provenance and raw evidence from a numerical score obtained by independent recomputation against references. WindPilot was then proposed as an execution framework that incorporates contract parsing, execution provenance, deterministic verification and bounded acceptance review into the LLM execution loop. On 30 OpenFOAM tasks with independent references, at least the structural maximum of 60 points was reached by a base agent on 28 tasks, but numerical credit was obtained on only 6. With the same model name and budget, WindPilot increased the number of tasks with numerical credit to 17, full-score tasks from 0 to 3 and the mean task score from 62.5 to 72.5. Mean action steps fell from 130.4 to 104.9, and mean token consumption decreased by 12.9%. The mean gain for atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) tasks was 18.5 points. A completed simulation run is therefore not sufficient for a usable urban wind result; usability depends on checks that tie reported metrics to raw evidence during execution.

title: What Transfers Across Cuneiform? Script-Level Substrate and Language-Specific Regularities via Segmentation and Representation
summary: Cuneiform recorded typologically unrelated languages for more than three millennia, raising a natural question: which of its statistical regularities are properties of the shared writing system, and which belong to individual languages? We answer this with two probe pairs targeting the same script-versus-language decomposition. The first compares two unsupervised, dictionary-free segmentation methods: transitional probability (TP), grounded in infant statistical-learning research, and Morfessor. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic evaluation of dictionary-free segmentation on cuneiform; the only prior published baseline relies on a hand-built dictionary (Max-Match, F1 = 0.74). Both our methods reach F1 > 0.97 within language (Morfessor reaches F1 > 0.99 on Akkadian and Sumerian), exceeding MaxMatch by more than 23 F1 points, but diverge sharply in cross-language transfer: TP holds F1 > 0.95 across all six language pairs, while Morfessor collapses to F1 = 0.27 from the 13K-token Elamite source. A learning curve and a Hittite stress test (34.7% foreign-script logograms, where TP drops 35 points and Morfessor only 8) further isolate the two underlying mechanisms. The second probe pair extends the same decomposition to representations: concatenating Unicode and Latin features improves classification in 11 of 12 morphosyntactic tasks (p < 0.01). We release CUNEI-TOOLS and a three-language benchmark.

title: HeteroWear: Sensor-Aware Self-Supervised Learning for Heterogeneous Wearable Activity Recognition
comment: Extended version of a paper accepted at IEEE BigData 2026. Code: https://github.com/yasamanmohammdpour/HeteroWear
summary: Self-supervised learning for wearable sensing is usually confined to a single dataset or device family, leaving open whether representations transfer across heterogeneous sensor configurations and whether gains come from pretraining rather than architecture or richer sensor input. We present HeteroWear, a sensor-aware self-supervised framework pretrained on an eight-dataset wearable corpus (173 subjects, 358,261 windows) spanning inertial and physiological signals across body locations, devices, and sampling rates. HeteroWear separates within-sensor temporal modeling from cross-sensor relational modeling using sensor-context embeddings, temporal and cross-sensor Transformers, and latent cross-attention fusion. Training combines structured sensor dropout, cross-configuration consistency, and per-axis masked sensor modeling; missing sensors are omitted rather than reconstructed. Under leave-one-dataset-out pretraining and subject-disjoint evaluation on PAMAP2, WISDM, HHAR, HARTH, and UCI-HAR, HeteroWear improves mean macro-F1 from 0.688 to 0.724 over the identical architecture trained from scratch, with the largest gain on HHAR (0.823 versus 0.741), and achieves the highest macro-F1 on four of five benchmarks relative to single-accelerometer supervised baselines. Held-out-device evaluation yields a mean +0.066 macro-F1 improvement. Under 50% test-time channel removal, HeteroWear retains 73.8% of full-channel performance versus 64.1% for the same architecture trained from scratch without sensor dropout. Ablations show that structured sensor dropout primarily drives robustness, while cross-configuration consistency and sensor-context encoding contribute to transfer.

title: SARGO: Agreement-Gated Reinforcement and Suppression via On-Policy Self-Guidance for Visual Hallucination Mitigation
summary: Vision-language models remain susceptible to visual hallucinations, often mixing grounded information with unsupported claims in the same response. Response-level reinforcement learning assigns a shared advantage to all tokens in a response, causing negative updates to suppress correct information alongside unsupported claims. To reduce hallucination while preserving useful visual information, we introduce SARGO (Self-guided Advantage-Routed Grounding Optimization), a post-training framework for selective reinforcement and suppression through on-policy self-guidance. Direct and reciprocal weighting gives better-supported tokens stronger reinforcement on positive updates and weaker penalties on negative updates. Agreement between overall and hallucination-specific advantages selects when to apply this guidance. At the response level, a reference-calibrated reward couples factuality with the retention and expansion of grounded information, discouraging lower hallucination scores obtained through omission. Experiments on Qwen3-VL-4B, Qwen3-VL-8B, and Gemma3-4B demonstrate that SARGO outperforms the evaluated mitigation baselines across Obj-Hal, AMBER, THRONE, and SHR evaluations. SARGO achieves these gains while preserving useful visual information and general multimodal capabilities.

title: EEGHyena2: Fixation-Inspired Joint Lexical-Grammatical Conditional Random Field for Interpretable EEG-to-Text Decoding
summary: A sentence is built from words that carry lexical meaning and grammatical roles, and brain activity during reading reflects both. Current EEG-to-text decoders, however, let a large language model (LLM) propose and order the words, so fluent output can reflect the LLM's prior more than the recorded EEG. In this study, we asked whether fixation-linked EEG carries lexical and grammatical evidence during natural reading and how a decoder can use such evidence. Fixation-related potential analyses showed that content and function words differ reliably in group-averaged EEG but only weakly in single words. We therefore propose EEGHyena2, a structured decoder in which a bidirectional encoder inspired by StripedHyena 2 feeds a semantic head that ranks a fixed lexicon and a part-of-speech (POS) head that predicts grammatical categories; a joint word-POS conditional random field (CRF) scores a restricted candidate lattice, and a frozen Llama-2 scores the candidates in context. On two natural-reading corpora, ZuCo and ROAMM, it matched the state-of-the-art method on BLEU-1 (21.4 vs 21.3), exceeded it on ROUGE-1 F1 (23.3 vs 20.3), lowered the character error rate on ROAMM (75.3% vs 84.7%) and decoded each recording about 3-10 times faster than LLM candidate search. The CRF learned transitions that mirror English syntax, and the encoder drew local context from its convolutions and distant context from attention. Decoders can thus pool weak word-level EEG evidence across the sentence through explicit lexical and grammatical structure, with the language model adjudicating among candidates rather than generating them, which lowers decoding cost and keeps decisions inspectable.

title: The Critic Can Hurt: On the Safety of Critics in LLM-Guided AutoML Search
summary: LLM critics increasingly steer iterative search in agentic AutoML, prompt optimization, and self-refinement--evaluated for whether they help, but rarely for whether they can hurt. We isolate the critic's marginal effect through a four-arm audit and characterize the loop's tolerance through controlled fault injection. We show a naive 8B critic drives search below the no-critic random-search floor on 7 of 8 tabular datasets, losing up to 0.245 AUC in the worst case; the magnitude varies strongly with dataset, frontier, and budget. When: stronger critics attenuate the loss on the evaluated suite, without establishing a universal capability threshold. Why: controlled fault injection shows that non-directional errors are nearly costless under best-so-far search, whereas directional errors consume finite search opportunities; an idealized effective-sample calculation yields a necessary condition, $q(m-1) > β$, not a deployment certificate. How: a simple observable validation gate and a learned detector can reduce realized loss, but neither is guaranteed to preserve the full-budget no-critic baseline. We will release CRITFAULT, to our knowledge the first benchmark for detecting harmful critic feedback in AutoML. A critic is not a free addition: audit before trusting, and gate when capability or verification is insufficient.

title: Confidence Without Cause: Predicting and Localizing Physics-Shortcut Sensitivity in Language Model Hidden States
summary: A language model's confidence on a physics problem deserves trust only if it ignores details irrelevant to the answer. We introduce DECOY (Distractor-Embedded Certified cOunterfactuals for phYsics): 155 families of four prompts differing in one irrelevant detail. A symbolic solver certifies that each edit preserves the answer. Families are labelled by the largest drop in the model's log-probability of the certified answer, using a threshold fixed before probe training. Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct is sensitive on 50.0% of the 140 families yielding labels, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on 22.9%. Effects are largest when distractor values lie numerically close to the answer. A linear probe on Qwen's layer-18 hidden state, averaged over four renderings, predicts sensitivity before generation at AUROC 0.760 with whole families held out. A separately tuned single-rendering probe reaches 0.747. A frozen layer-16 probe reaches 0.820 pooled AUROC on 15 families built after training, though within-cue-type AUROC is lower (0.667-0.6875). Under a paired family bootstrap, the probe performs on par with a fitted token-entropy baseline (AUROC 0.727) and achieves the lowest Brier score among tested predictors (0.204 versus 0.214). Knocking out four attention heads at layer 16 cancels sensitivity on a 20-family panel, localising it to a narrow mechanism. These results show that Qwen's confidence can track irrelevant details, that this failure is detectable before generation, and that targeted intervention can suppress it. DECOY provides certified ground truth and paired-tested baselines for evaluating hidden-state monitors.

title: Latency, Speech Recognition and Turn-Taking in Voice Agents for Spanish Phone Negotiation: An Externally Measured Comparison of Pipecat, LiveKit and GPT-Live
comment: 12 pages, 6 figures, 11 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/AILabFr8tech/voice-negotiation-agents (archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24211550)
summary: A voice agent that negotiates by phone must answer quickly, understand spoken amounts and cope with a caller who talks over it. We compared three architectures for such an agent, negotiating freight rates in Spanish: two cascades (speech recognition, language model and speech synthesis) orchestrated by Pipecat and by LiveKit Agents, and GPT-Live, an OpenAI speech model that listens and speaks without separate stages. A program played the carrier with the same 47 recordings of one speaker for all agents, without the telephone network, in 77 calls per architecture over five negotiation scenarios, and measured latency on the listener's side with a validated instrument. Median latency to the content response was 2,616.0 ms (Pipecat), 3,090.0 ms (LiveKit) and 2,444.8 ms (GPT-Live); the confidence interval of GPT-Live's 171.2 ms advantage over Pipecat includes zero. According to its own timestamps, GPT-Live began to answer 800 ms after the end of the line, close to the 0.8 s published by OpenAI; most of the remaining wait, about 1,367 ms and nearly constant, is the audio's round trip through OpenAI's service. A tool call added 0.9-1.1 s in every architecture, more than any difference between them, and the frameworks' self-reported latency fell short of the listener's wait by 9% (Pipecat) and 22% (LiveKit). Word error rates were low (6.03, 4.93 and 1.47%), but the error on amounts was 13.01% and 12.61% in the cascades, against 2.86% in GPT-Live. With default settings, Pipecat and LiveKit stopped at almost every backchannel and often took it as the carrier's answer: an "ok" spoken over the agent ended in a registered agreement in 3 of 15 Pipecat calls, 2 of 15 LiveKit calls and no GPT-Live call (descriptive counts, not tested). Latency should therefore be measured on the listener's side, and a cascade needs safeguards for spoken amounts and backchannels.

title: Understanding the Role of Reasoning Data in Pretraining
summary: Reasoning data expose models to multi-step reasoning, but reasoning traces may cover only a subset of the available facts. How should pretraining balance atomic facts with reasoning traces? We study this question by constructing a setting in which every fact provides an atomic training signal, while only a subset appears in reasoning supervision, enabling us to measure generalization to transitions observed atomically but never used in training traces. For a linear transformer, we derive the weight assigned to atomic training signals that minimizes held-transition squared error and show that its leading-order optimum increases with reasoning-chain length and decreases with the fraction of facts held out from reasoning traces. These trends persist in a full transformer layer with an MLP, softmax attention, and cross-entropy loss. We further validate the role of reasoning complexity and data coverage in two natural-language settings: controlled multi-hop reasoning and mathematical pretraining. Together, our results provide a principled view of how reasoning-chain structure and data coverage should shape the allocation of training data during pretraining.

title: PMR: MoE Routing with Shared Prototypes and Congestion Pricing
summary: Conventional linear routers in sparse mixture-of-experts models select experts directly from token-expert matching scores, coupling input matching with expert allocation. We propose Prototype-Mediated Routing (PMR), a two-stage router with shared prototypes. PMR first computes each token's distribution over prototypes, then uses it to mix prototype-conditioned expert distributions according to the law of total probability. This formulation models input matching and expert allocation separately, explicitly represents many-to-many associations between prototypes and experts, and provides separate interfaces for context adaptation and load regulation. Within this framework, short-term states summarize preceding tokens to adapt the prototypes, while congestion prices updated from dispatch feedback achieve loss-free load balancing by adjusting the conditional expert distributions. We use a two-pass blockwise approximation to accelerate short-term state processing, achieving over 20 times the training throughput of the eager tokenwise PMR implementation while maintaining high agreement in routing decisions. Across three pretraining configurations with 0.43B, 1.18B, and 0.48B total parameters, PMR improves mean zero-shot accuracy on seven benchmarks over linear routing baselines with matched expert architectures by 1.54, 2.65, and 1.45 percentage points (pp), respectively. The corresponding gains on ARC-Easy are 6.71, 5.80, and 3.92 pp. In parameter-efficient fine-tuning of 7B-8B backbones, PMR's improvements over MixLoRA vary across backbones, with gains of up to 1.76 pp in mean accuracy across four tasks.

title: Low-Latency LLM-Based Streaming Multi-Talker ASR with Verifiable Rewards
summary: LLM-based architectures offer strong generalization and instruction-following capabilities for streaming automatic speech recognition (ASR), but multi-talker use introduces coupled transcription, attribution, and latency challenges. Our wearable setting requires real-time transcription of a conversation between a near-field device wearer and a far-field partner. Because partial hypotheses are rendered on persistent sides of a dialogue UI, speaker roles cannot be permuted and each speaker tag must precede its turn. These sparse tags are weakly optimized by supervised fine-tuning (SFT), while committing to a leading tag can delay the text that follows. We therefore post-train a streaming LLM-based ASR model with reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), combining a fixed-role Speaker-Attributed WER (SA-WER) grader with a turn-level onset-delay reward. On an eight-direction multi-talker cohort, SA-WER RL reduces SA-WER from $20.51\%$ for SFT to $13.14\%$. Adding the delay objective reduces onset $p50$ by $65\%$ (from $0.918\,\text{s}$ to $0.320\,\text{s}$) and $p90$ by $44\%$ (from $1.389\,\text{s}$ to $0.780\,\text{s}$) relative to SA-WER-only RL, while achieving $12.70\%$ SA-WER. These results demonstrate that fixed-role recognition quality and streaming responsiveness can be improved jointly.

title: A Fast Algorithm for the Familywise Loss
summary: The familywise (FW) loss for multiclass classification, introduced by Duchi, Ruan, and Khosravi, achieves universal equivalence to the 0-1 loss, and thus has stronger theoretical properties than cross entropy (CE). Prior work, however, left open whether FW is as computationally efficient as CE. First, on the theoretical side, we prove that the FW gradient can be computed in $O(K)$ time, where $K$ is the number of classes. Second, on the practical side, we develop optimized kernels for computing the forward and backward passes of FW which outperform CE in terms of speed on both CPU and GPU.

title: Program Distillation: Transferring LLM Capability from System 2 to System 0
summary: Recent studies leverage large language models (LLMs) to construct executable programs through environment interaction, feedback analysis, and code revision. However, prior work has mainly treated LLMs as optimizers, overlooking their ability to transfer knowledge across system levels. We propose Program Distillation (PD), a framework that formalizes the transfer of abilities from System 2 to System 0. During learning, the LLM provides task knowledge and draft strategies; at deployment, a student program executes the resulting policy. We show that this approach can improve performance while reducing inference time. We introduce PDBench, a benchmark comprising 27 discrete- and continuous-control tasks with fixed initial policies, and PDMetaHarness, a model-harness-independent meta-system for monitoring and guiding the learning process. The strongest model achieves a normalized mean score of 0.728, surpassing PPO (0.656) and Jev-like decision models (0.239), while running exclusively on CPUs and reducing inference costs. Our analysis shows that performance is largely driven by the first breakthrough during learning, and structural modifications have a slightly lower success rate than parameter modifications but typically yield larger gains. We further introduce style distillation, which enables interpretable stylistic control over the learning process. Overall, we present an analytical framework for PD and demonstrate its practical viability.

title: A Systematic Study of Cross-Token Transfer for Data-Efficient Non-Verbal Text-to-Speech
summary: Non-verbal vocalizations (NVs), such as laughter and breath, carry affective cues that words alone do not convey. Yet NV data remains scarce because speech annotation pipelines often omit or normalize these events. Existing work has improved NV text-to-speech through model design and data curation, but whether one NV token can help a model learn another has received little systematic study. We investigate this cross-token transferability in a controlled CosyVoice 2 setup. We first trace a laughter-only scaling curve, then hold laughter at 200 or 1,600 examples while adding breath, sigh, cough, lip-smack, or neutral speech. With only 200 laughter examples, adding 3,200 cough examples raises end-to-end laughter F1 from 0.170 to 0.529, surpassing the 0.495 obtained from 1,600 laughter examples alone. At the 1,600-example anchor, cough reaches 0.695, nearly matching 6,400 laughter examples (0.697). Waveform-level Whisper-D scoring and a semantic-token transcriber show consistent trends. Cross-token transfer therefore offers a complementary route to low-resource NV generation.

title: Nahual: A Sequence Model for Language and Atoms
summary: Generative models play a rapidly growing role in the design and simulation of molecules. The most widely used applications of generative models are in large language models (LLMs), owing to the natural flexibility of language for specifying and answering queries. However, generalist LLMs do not effectively handle large sets of 3D coordinates, whereas specialist generative models of 3D molecules cannot reach the controllability afforded by language. To bridge these capabilities, we propose Nahual, a decoder-only autoregressive diffusion model for any sequence of text and 3D molecules. To enable expressive autoregression on continuous coordinates, we propose next-token diffusion, whereby a causal transformer denoises each token while attending to the clean tokens before it, without increasing context size. We train Nahual on a curated set of twelve 3D chemistry tasks ranging from microsolvation to molecular conformer search to adsorption on metal surfaces, with associated evaluation metrics and baselines. The result is a single set of end-to-end-trained weights that simultaneously performs all tasks and surpasses state-of-the-art models specialized for crystal structure prediction and property-conditional molecule generation. Our results demonstrate the viability of scaling generalist decoder-only models for native multimodal understanding and generation across language and chemistry. Code is available at https://github.com/the-matter-lab/nahual.

title: Objectify, Don't Delete: Complaint-Derived Evaluation of Ambient Clinical Notes
comment: Accepted at the Third Workshop on GenAI for Health (GenAI4Health), NeurIPS 2026 (non-archival). 16 pages, 5 figures, 11 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/nikita0511/aci-defect
summary: Evaluating the quality of AI-generated clinical notes is hard: standard metrics like ROUGE measure lexical similarity to reference notes, while expert checklists encode what committees believe matters. Neither captures what clinicians actually complain about. Recent work has shown that evaluation criteria can be mined from user feedback and filtered to criteria that LLM judges can reliably enforce. We argue that this is where much of the value is lost. The criteria that fail enforceability are disproportionately the ones clinicians raise most often, because high-frequency complaints are stated as several questions glued together. No yes/no judgment can grade such composites as posed. We introduce an objectification step that rewrites such criteria into sets of scoped, determinate decisions. We demonstrate the approach through an evaluation pipeline that mines criteria from complaints, objectifies them, and deploys LLM judges against both planted defects and production notes. Across eleven defects planted into ACI-bench reference notes, objectified judges localize violations with median recall of 0.95, while reference metrics change by at most 0.037. Given the complaint as one broad question, the same judges still find every planted defect, but they also flag 70% of the unperturbed reference notes; one section-pair question per call raises Youden's J from 0.30 to 0.72 (by 0.19 to 0.26 with prompt effort matched). We release ACI-Defect, a perturbation benchmark; clinician-reviewed instance-level labels showing quality gaps in the ACI-bench gold standard (32 of 40 notes contain hallucinations; 40 of 40 omit discussed facts); and grounding-judge verdicts. On 1,446 production notes, mean instance-rate burden falls at every clinician-rating step (rho=-0.15), a small association. Defect counts have to be kept per span rather than collapsed into one pass/fail bit per note.

title: MarineSparkLM-4B: A Lightweight Language Model for Marine and Offshore Engineering Built by Parameter-Efficient Adaptation
summary: Marine and offshore engineering text is spread across preprints, open-access journals, encyclopedias and institutional documents, and the amount of it is small by pretraining standards. We ask how far a lightweight language model for marine and offshore engineering can be taken with parameter-efficient adaptation on a single workstation-class device. Starting from the 4-billion-parameter OceanGPT-basic-4B-Instruct, we train two independent LoRA adapters, each updating 33.0 million of 4.06 billion parameters (0.81%). Training took 4 hours 40 minutes for the first adapter and 10 minutes for the second on one NVIDIA DGX Spark. The first adapter is trained by next-token prediction on a 61.6-million-token corpus covering ten engineering themes. The corpus was built from 13,879 source documents, of which 7,069 were retained after deduplication and a two-tier keyword filter that removes cross-domain lexical collisions. Its validation loss falls from 2.082 to 1.976 over 1,500 steps. Direct testing showed that this adapter could still drift off topic on a retrieval-grounded ballast-water prompt, so we trained a second adapter on 2,295 question-answer pairs (114 hand-written and 2,181 generated by the base model from corpus passages) with the loss restricted to answer tokens. On 20 held-out prompts scored by hand for accuracy, topicality and specificity (maximum 120), the plain base model, the continuation adapter, the instruction adapter and the instruction adapter with retrieval scored 42, 56, 84 and 88. Absolute accuracy stays low (14 of 40 without retrieval and 20 of 40 with it). We report the full pipeline, two negative results (a reverted keyword fix and an instruction run that overfit within 100 steps), and the limits of the evaluation, which uses one small prompt set, no inter-rater agreement measure and model-generated reference answers.

title: DynaDFlash: Dynamic Feature Projection for Block Diffusion Speculators
comment: Code and trained models available at https://github.com/midas-llm-research/DynaDFlash
summary: DFlash trains a parallel draft model on hidden features from its target model. Inspired by the previous work of DFlare that introduced per layer combinations of target hidden states, we test whether context dependent weighting of these states helps improve acceptance length of block diffusion speculators. We trained both a DFlash baseline for the Qwen 3 of block size 16, and a dynamic model that computes gates for each layer to affect the magnitude of hidden features before projection. While mean acceptance length between the dynamic model and the DFlash baseline didn't significantly differ, we notice that the dynamic model excels for drafting in the context of math. In an evaluation of 700 prompts from the MetaMathQA and Orca-Math datasets, the mean accepted length improves by 5%. We also found this lead to a 4.1% higher throughput for a subset of the same dataset in the context of speculative decoding.

title: Ultra-CAN: A Lightweight Blind ISAC Receiver for Chaos-Based Telemetry and Local-Seed Ranging in the Internet of Drones
comment: 14 pages, 6 figures, 9 tables. Submitted to IEEE Internet of Things Journal
summary: The Internet of Drones (IoD) needs secure telemetry and proximity sensing within the SWaP-C constraints. We show that a single blind neural receiver driven by one chaos-based waveform performs both functions without a separate radar transceiver. In telemetry mode it decodes a peer's burst blindly; in radar mode it regenerates the per-burst chaotic reference locally and ranges the echoes of its own transmission. Ultra-CAN pairs a shared $64$-dimensional representation with two ultra-light backbones, an attention-pooled Conv1D network and a multi-head QKV network ($27.6$k--$44.2$k parameters), feeding communication and sensing heads. Both ship as int8 TensorFlow Lite Micro firmware; the Conv1D receiver decides a burst in $16.9$ ms on a $240$ MHz microcontroller with $24.2$ KiB of activations, a measured energy of $2.2$-$3.4$ mJ per burst, and float-equivalent decisions, sustaining up to $59$ bit/s of telemetry or a $7.4$ Hz range track. The two variants rank first and second among learned demodulators in four aerial swarm scenarios, with a pooled BER down to $4.6 \times 10^{-4}$ on the single-echo link ($2.4 \times 10^{-3}$ with three echoes). Its sensing head identifies true obstacles in $66.8\%$ of peer-laden bursts (vs $42\%$ matched filtering, $44\%$ OFDM-ISAC, $48\%$ peak-picker ceiling). A peer-exclusion gate cuts peer reports from $4.4\%$ to $0.02\%$ of answered bursts, answering $23.5\%$ of total bursts ($75\%$ on the exact tap) with $0.70$ m/s velocity tracking. In-domain refitting recovers telemetry BER by up to three orders of magnitude under 3GPP channels, jamming-aware training restores the link, and frequency agility adds a $6$--$9$ dB margin against partial-band jamming.

title: Personalized Language Models for One-to-Many Private Communications
summary: We study relationship-specific continual reply prediction for one-to-many private communication: a system predicts an author's reply to a recurring contact and updates its personalization state when the actual reply becomes available. We propose TRACE (Temporal Relationship-Aware Communication Evolution), which uses author-level lexical habits, contact-specific wording, and temporal expression estimates to guide a frozen language model, with a feedback-driven policy controlling revision. On 216 test emails from eight Enron users, all four main TRACE configurations achieve higher mean BLEU, ROUGE-L, and BERTScore and lower mean Reply Style MSE than Base LLM and Base RAG. Component ablations show mixed effects and do not establish statistically reliable improvements in Reply Style MSE after multiple-comparison correction. More accurate state forecasts and larger revision budgets do not consistently improve reply-level metrics. These exploratory findings expose the challenge of turning evolving relationship-specific expression estimates into useful generation guidance.

title: Knowledge-Guided Local-to-Global Anomaly Learning for Longitudinal Medication Trajectories
summary: Detecting suspicious deviations in longitudinal medication trajectories requires distinguishing knowledge-consistent treatment variations from anomalous changes and linking local deviations to account-level decisions. We propose a knowledge-guided local-to-global (L2G) anomaly learning framework that addresses both challenges. It constructs proxy supervision at three granularities: medication occurrences, treatment episodes, and contiguous visit segments. Knowledge-consistent medication and episode replacements provide plausible negatives, while cross-category and cross-account perturbations provide suspicious proxies. A medication-multiset encoder and causal visit-sequence encoder feed a shared scoring head that produces visit-level anomaly logits. Top-\(α\) aggregation derives account-level scores from these logits, while account-level classification and class-balanced visit-localization objectives jointly optimize the same visit-level evidence. Experiments on two city cohorts compare L2G with native and proxy-adapted anomaly methods. On City-A, L2G outperforms the strongest comparators. Cross-city results show more consistent gains in localization than in account-level detection.

title: Empowering Masked Diffusion Models to Self-Correct with Leave-One-Out Transformers
summary: Masked diffusion models (MDMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for language modeling, enabling parallel token generation with competitive performance. Yet standard MDMs suffer from two fundamental limitations: (1) inability to revise tokens, and (2) sparse training signal. We revisit hollow transformers, which address both limitations by predicting each token from its surrounding context, independently of the input at that position. We introduce the Leave-One-Out Transformer (LOOT), a more efficient and expressive architecture that advances hollow transformers through two complementary advances.
